messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Vignette:
Daniel is a 55-year-old fashion designer who came to treatment after years of arranging his life around a sense of danger he could never fully explain, even to himself. He was raised by a caregiver who physically abused him throughout childhood. When he tries to describe those years, the account breaks apart. He can circle details—the feel of being cornered in a quiet house, the sudden movement before a blow, the watchfulness he learned in rooms where nothing was being said—but he cannot put it into a single clear sequence. At times he speaks about it in a flat, almost detached way, as if he were describing something that happened to another boy. At other moments, a memory arrives with crushing guilt, and he is left dwelling on what he believes he did wrong, what he should have anticipated, how he might have prevented what happened. Just as often, his mind turns outward and fixes on what was done to him, replaying the cruelty and the unfairness of it until he feels consumed by the injuries other people have caused.

What remains most vivid is not a neatly told story but a way of sensing danger. As a child, silence in the house did not mean peace. Silence meant waiting, listening, bracing for the next shift in mood or the next approach. That association has stayed with him into adult life. In his apartment now, unusual quiet can make his body tense before he has consciously registered why. He finds himself listening for footsteps, for a door, for some sign that something bad is about to happen. Even at home, where he knows he is alone and should be able to relax, he feels on guard. He checks locks more than once and remains alert to small sounds, as though safety could vanish without warning.

This constant readiness follows him into work. Daniel has built a respected career in fashion, a profession that places him in studios, fitting rooms, crowded workspaces, and backstage environments where people move quickly and touch without much ceremony. A hand landing unexpectedly on his shoulder when a seamstress is asking a question, or a model brushing past him from behind, can make him jolt with visible alarm. He knows these moments are ordinary in his field, and the embarrassment afterward is often sharp. He worries that colleagues notice his reaction and think there is something deeply wrong with him. He has begun positioning himself at the edge of rooms, preferring to see people approach. In fittings he is careful about where he stands, less because he can explain it than because it feels intolerable to be surprised by contact.

Over the years he has come to believe that the abuse permanently changed him for the worse. He does not speak about this dramatically; rather, it appears in the certainty with which he dismisses the possibility of feeling normal. He says he has never really trusted people and does not see why he should. Being close to others feels risky, not only in intimate relationships—his marriage ended years ago—but in ordinary dependence, in letting anyone see uncertainty or need. He is also frightened by his own reactions. The startle, the scanning, the way a quiet evening can suddenly feel ominous, the way memories arrive either numb or unbearable—these have led him to wonder if he is going crazy.

He has developed small but rigid habits around sleep. Because certain times of day and evening conditions seem to bring on nightmares, he tries to avoid them indirectly: keeping the television on late, staying busy, stretching work into the night, resisting the transition into bed when he senses the familiar dread building. These routines leave him tired and frayed, but he clings to them because they feel like the only available defense. In the hours when he cannot distract himself, his mind turns over the same questions: what others did to him, what he failed to do, how much of his life has been shaped by damage he cannot undo.

He sought help now after a recent period of mounting strain at work and at home. In the studio, he startled so violently when an assistant touched him from behind that everyone stopped and stared. Later that week, alone in his apartment, the silence of the place became so threatening that he left the television and lights on in every room just to get through the evening. What finally brought him in was less one dramatic incident than the fear that his world had narrowed to managing reactions he did not understand. He wants, cautiously, to know whether there is a way to live without being on guard all the time. What frightens him most is the possibility that this is all he will ever be now: damaged, mistrustful, and losing control of his own mind.
